prompt: Which of the following best explains how a public policy can promote long-run economic growth?

options.label: A
options.text: It can permanently raise real GDP per capita by increasing the price level alone

options.label: B
options.text: It can raise productivity or labor-force participation, increasing real GDP per capita over time

options.label: C
options.text: It can increase nominal GDP while leaving productive capacity and real output unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: It can guarantee growth whenever government spending rises, regardless of what the spending finances

options.label: E
options.text: It can create long-run growth only by reducing the number of people participating in the labor force

explanation: Policies that raise productivity or labor-force participation can increase the amount of real output produced per person. The CED links these channels directly to real GDP per capita and economic growth.

prompt: A government program that successfully raises worker productivity will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Increase long-run real GDP only if the overall price level rises by the same percentage

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce potential output because higher productivity lowers the number of inputs required per unit

options.label: C
options.text: Leave economic growth unchanged because public policy cannot affect productive capacity

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the economy’s capacity to produce real output and support higher real GDP per capita

options.label: E
options.text: Increase nominal output while necessarily leaving real GDP per capita unchanged

explanation: Higher productivity means a given quantity of labor and other resources can produce more real output. If population is unchanged, that improvement can raise real GDP per capita and support economic growth.

prompt: Which public policy would most directly increase labor-force participation?

options.label: A
options.text: A policy that strengthens the incentive or ability of nonworkers to enter the labor force

options.label: B
options.text: A policy that raises the price level without changing work incentives or employment opportunities

options.label: C
options.text: A policy that reduces worker productivity while leaving the size of the labor force unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: A policy that replaces private investment with government consumption and does not alter work decisions

options.label: E
options.text: A policy that raises nominal wages only because the general price level increased

explanation: Labor-force participation rises when more working-age people choose and are able to participate in the labor market. Policies that change work incentives or remove barriers to participation can therefore affect growth through the labor-input channel.

prompt: Which of the following is the clearest example of a government policy that can raise long-run growth through infrastructure investment?

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing transfer payments that are used entirely for current consumption

options.label: B
options.text: Purchasing existing financial assets without changing productive resources or technology

options.label: C
options.text: Raising the price level through policies that do not change productive capacity

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing the number of usable roads and ports available to private producers

options.label: E
options.text: Constructing transportation and communications networks that make private production more efficient

explanation: Infrastructure such as transportation and communications systems can make labor and capital more productive. By improving the efficiency of production, public infrastructure can raise potential output and long-run growth.

prompt: Government investment in new technology can promote economic growth primarily by

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing the price level so that nominal GDP rises even if real output does not

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing the economy’s capital stock to encourage firms to use more labor

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing productivity so that more real output can be produced with available resources

options.label: D
options.text: Decreasing labor-force participation so output is divided among fewer workers

options.label: E
options.text: Creating a permanent increase in aggregate demand without affecting productive capacity

explanation: Technological improvement raises the productivity of resources. More output can then be produced from a given quantity of inputs, increasing potential output and supporting growth in real GDP per capita.

prompt: Supply-side fiscal policies are best described as fiscal policies that

options.label: A
options.text: Change the money supply in order to influence short-run nominal interest rates

options.label: B
options.text: Affect only aggregate demand and have no possible effect on productive capacity

options.label: C
options.text: Change productive incentives, aggregate supply, and potential output

options.label: D
options.text: Set the equilibrium real interest rate directly in the loanable funds market

options.label: E
options.text: Change the price level without influencing household or business economic behavior

explanation: Supply-side fiscal policies operate through incentives that affect household and business decisions, such as work and investment. Because those decisions influence productive capacity, the policies can affect aggregate supply and potential output as well as aggregate demand.

prompt: A reduction in a marginal tax rate is most likely to be considered supply-side fiscal policy when it is intended to

options.label: A
options.text: Increase incentives to work, save, invest, or undertake other productive economic activity

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce the money supply by lowering the quantity of bank reserves

options.label: C
options.text: Move the economy along an unchanged LRAS curve by raising the price level

options.label: D
options.text: Decrease potential output while increasing only current consumption

options.label: E
options.text: Eliminate the distinction between nominal and real GDP

explanation: A supply-side tax change is aimed at changing incentives that shape productive behavior. If after-tax rewards to work or investment rise, labor supply or capital formation may increase and potential output can rise.

prompt: Based on the graph above, which public policy is most consistent with the change from PPC1 to PPC2?

options.label: A
options.text: A temporary increase in household consumption that moves production along PPC1

options.label: B
options.text: A policy that raises the price level while leaving resources and technology unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: A decline in labor-force participation that reduces the quantity of labor available

options.label: D
options.text: A reduction in productive technology that makes existing resources less efficient

options.label: E
options.text: A productive infrastructure program that increases the economy’s capacity to produce both goods

explanation: An outward shift of the PPC represents an increase in productive capacity. Infrastructure that makes production more efficient can expand the economy’s feasible output combinations and therefore support economic growth.
graphDescription: Capital goods are on the horizontal axis and consumer goods are on the vertical axis. PPC2 lies outside PPC1 at every relevant combination, and an arrow indicates an outward shift associated with infrastructure investment.

prompt: Which policy is most directly aimed at raising long-run growth through technological progress?

options.label: A
options.text: A transfer program that raises current spending without changing technology or productive resources

options.label: B
options.text: Government funding that supports research and development leading to more productive technologies

options.label: C
options.text: A temporary price subsidy that only raises purchases of existing consumer goods

options.label: D
options.text: A policy that lowers labor-force participation while leaving productivity unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: A policy that increases nominal GDP solely through a higher general price level

explanation: Public support for research and development can generate technological improvements that raise productivity.

prompt: A government program that improves worker training is most likely to promote economic growth by

options.label: A
options.text: Raising nominal wages without increasing the real output workers can produce

options.label: B
options.text: Shifting aggregate demand left while leaving productive capacity unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: Reducing the economy’s available stock of knowledge and technology

options.label: D
options.text: Raising human capital and therefore increasing labor productivity

options.label: E
options.text: Lowering the participation of trained workers in the labor force

explanation: Training can increase workers’ skills and knowledge, which raises human capital. More productive workers can produce more output per unit of labor, supporting higher potential output and real GDP per capita.

prompt: A policy that makes it easier for working-age adults to enter employment can affect economic growth by

options.label: A
options.text: Reducing the economy’s productive resources and shifting potential output left

options.label: B
options.text: Raising the price level without altering the quantity of labor available

options.label: C
options.text: Decreasing total output because more people are counted in the labor force

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing labor-force participation and the amount of labor available for production

options.label: E
options.text: Changing nominal GDP while necessarily leaving real GDP per capita unchanged

explanation: A higher labor-force participation rate can increase the labor input used in production. With other determinants held constant, more employed labor can increase real output and contribute to higher real GDP per capita.

prompt: An investment tax credit intended to encourage firms to purchase new productive capital is a supply-side policy because it can

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce the monetary base and thereby lower the quantity of money supplied

options.label: B
options.text: Increase current consumption while necessarily reducing the future capital stock

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the incentive for business investment and expand future productive capacity

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the price level without influencing investment incentives

options.label: E
options.text: Decrease the after-tax return on productive capital and reduce potential output

explanation: An investment tax credit raises the after-tax attractiveness of acquiring productive capital.

prompt: In the short run, a tax cut that raises household disposable income will most directly tend to

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease consumption and shift aggregate demand to the left

options.label: B
options.text: Increase consumption and shift aggregate demand to the right

options.label: C
options.text: Shift LRAS to the left solely because households have more disposable income

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce the price level without changing aggregate demand

options.label: E
options.text: Decrease the incentive to work by lowering the after-tax return to labor in every case

explanation: A tax cut can raise disposable income and consumption, creating a short-run demand-side effect. Supply-side fiscal policy can therefore affect aggregate demand even when its longer-run objective is to influence productive incentives.

prompt: Based on the graph above, which outcome is most consistent with a successful policy that raises economy-wide productivity?

options.label: A
options.text: The full-employment level of real GDP increases from Yf1 to Yf2

options.label: B
options.text: The economy moves upward along LRAS1 because the price level rises

options.label: C
options.text: Potential output falls from Yf2 to Yf1 because productivity increased

options.label: D
options.text: The price level alone increases while the full-employment output level remains fixed

options.label: E
options.text: Aggregate demand shifts left while productive capacity is necessarily unchanged

explanation: Higher productivity increases the amount of real output the economy can sustain at full employment. On the AD-AS model, that increase in potential output is represented by a rightward shift of LRAS.
graphDescription: Price level is on the vertical axis and real GDP is on the horizontal axis. LRAS1 is vertical at Yf1 and LRAS2 is vertical farther to the right at Yf2; an arrow points from LRAS1 to LRAS2.

prompt: A new public highway system can raise productivity when it

options.label: A
options.text: Raises the price level without changing production costs or delivery times

options.label: B
options.text: Reduces access to markets and makes existing capital less useful

options.label: C
options.text: Causes firms to use fewer productive technologies than before

options.label: D
options.text: Lowers labor-force participation while leaving output per worker unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: Reduces transportation time and costs for workers and firms

explanation: Infrastructure can raise productivity by reducing the resources needed to move goods, workers, and information.

prompt: If a supply-side fiscal policy successfully increases potential output, which curve will most directly reflect that long-run change?

options.label: A
options.text: The long-run aggregate supply curve shifts to the right

options.label: B
options.text: The aggregate demand curve shifts left with no change in aggregate supply

options.label: C
options.text: The money demand curve shifts right because potential output increased

options.label: D
options.text: The short-run Phillips curve becomes vertical at the new price level

options.label: E
options.text: The loanable-funds supply curve becomes perfectly horizontal

explanation: Potential output is represented by the position of LRAS.

prompt: Which policy is least likely to be classified as supply-side fiscal policy?

options.label: A
options.text: A tax incentive intended to encourage firms to invest in productive capital

options.label: B
options.text: A tax change intended to increase households’ incentive to participate in the labor force

options.label: C
options.text: A public investment program that expands productive infrastructure

options.label: D
options.text: A technology program intended to raise productivity in private production

options.label: E
options.text: A one-time transfer payment designed only to raise current household spending

explanation: A one-time transfer aimed solely at current spending operates primarily through aggregate demand and does not necessarily change productive incentives. Supply-side policies are specifically aimed at behavior that can affect aggregate supply or potential output.

prompt: Holding productivity constant, an increase in labor-force participation can support long-run growth because it

options.label: A
options.text: Reduces the economy’s labor input and lowers full-employment output

options.label: B
options.text: Raises nominal GDP only through a higher price level

options.label: C
options.text: Causes an inward shift of the production possibilities curve

options.label: D
options.text: Expands the labor available for producing goods and services

options.label: E
options.text: Necessarily reduces real GDP per capita whenever more people work

explanation: Greater labor-force participation expands the labor input available for production. With productivity unchanged, a larger employed share of the population can raise total real output and real GDP per capita.

prompt: A reduction in the marginal tax rate on labor income may increase potential output if it

options.label: A
options.text: Lowers the after-tax reward to work and reduces the labor input

options.label: B
options.text: Raises only the overall price level while leaving labor decisions unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: Raises the after-tax reward to work and increases labor-force participation

options.label: D
options.text: Reduces worker productivity by increasing the amount of human capital

options.label: E
options.text: Decreases aggregate supply because more people choose to enter the labor force

explanation: A lower marginal tax rate can increase the reward from earning additional income. If that change encourages more labor-force participation or work effort, the economy’s labor input and potential output can rise.

prompt: A policy that encourages firms to add productive machinery can increase economic growth primarily by

options.label: A
options.text: Reducing the physical capital stock so workers rely more heavily on labor

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing physical capital available to workers and raising productive capacity

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the price level while holding real productive resources constant

options.label: D
options.text: Decreasing productivity because machines substitute for some worker tasks

options.label: E
options.text: Reducing the potential output that can be produced at full employment

explanation: Additional productive capital gives workers more or better tools with which to produce.

prompt: Which public policy would most directly target productivity rather than labor-force participation?

options.label: A
options.text: A work-support policy intended to encourage nonworkers to seek employment

options.label: B
options.text: A tax change designed specifically to increase the reward from entering the labor force

options.label: C
options.text: A childcare program whose stated objective is to enable more adults to work

options.label: D
options.text: A hiring subsidy intended mainly to draw additional workers into employment

options.label: E
options.text: A program financing research that improves production technology

explanation: Technology policy operates primarily through productivity by improving how efficiently inputs are transformed into output.

prompt: Based on the graph above, which statement best describes the policy shown?

options.label: A
options.text: The policy reduces both aggregate demand and productive capacity at the same time

options.label: B
options.text: Raises current aggregate demand and expands future productive capacity

options.label: C
options.text: The policy changes only the price level and leaves all macroeconomic curves fixed

options.label: D
options.text: The policy shifts aggregate demand right but necessarily shifts potential output left

options.label: E
options.text: The policy increases productive capacity only by shifting aggregate demand farther right

explanation: Supply-side fiscal policy can have both demand-side and supply-side effects. A tax incentive or productive public investment can raise current spending while also improving incentives, productivity, or capacity over time.
graphDescription: Price level is on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis. The graph shows AD2 to the right of AD1, SRAS2 to the right of SRAS1, and LRAS2 to the right of LRAS1.

prompt: Supply-side fiscal policy affects potential output by influencing

options.label: A
options.text: The accounting definition of real GDP without changing actual economic behavior

options.label: B
options.text: The money supply directly through commercial bank reserve creation

options.label: C
options.text: Household and business incentives related to work, saving, investment, and productive activity

options.label: D
options.text: Only the current price level, with no effect on resource use or productivity

options.label: E
options.text: The nominal value of output while productive capacity remains permanently unchanged

explanation: The defining mechanism of supply-side fiscal policy is its effect on incentives.

prompt: A government technology program that makes existing capital more productive will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease potential output because each unit of capital is used more intensively

options.label: B
options.text: Increase only nominal output because technology cannot affect real production

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce labor productivity while leaving potential output unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: Raises productive capacity by making existing resources more productive

options.label: E
options.text: Shift the PPC inward because fewer resources are needed for each unit of output

explanation: Better technology raises the efficiency with which resources are used. This allows the economy to produce more real output with the same underlying resources and therefore expands productive capacity.

prompt: Which outcome would provide the strongest evidence that a public policy affected long-run economic growth rather than only short-run spending?

options.label: A
options.text: Potential output and real GDP per capita rise through greater productive capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Nominal GDP rises because the price level increases while real output is unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: Consumption increases for one quarter while the economy’s productive capacity is unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: Aggregate demand rises temporarily but LRAS remains at the same full-employment output

options.label: E
options.text: Government purchases increase while productivity and labor-force participation remain unchanged

explanation: Long-run growth requires an increase in productive capacity and is measured through real GDP per capita. A temporary increase in spending alone can raise current output without increasing the economy’s long-run capacity.

prompt: Government spending on a new freight rail network can have which pair of effects?

options.label: A
options.text: It can lower aggregate demand during construction and reduce productive capacity after completion

options.label: B
options.text: It can raise the price level but cannot affect productivity or potential output

options.label: C
options.text: Raises demand during construction and productive capacity through improved infrastructure

options.label: D
options.text: It can increase labor-force participation only, without changing productivity or infrastructure

options.label: E
options.text: It can reduce both current spending and the efficiency of private production

explanation: Infrastructure spending is itself part of aggregate demand in the short run. If the completed infrastructure makes private production more efficient, it can also raise productivity and potential output in the longer run.

prompt: Public investment in education can support economic growth when it

options.label: A
options.text: Raises the price level without changing worker skills or productive capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Reduces the stock of human capital available to employers

options.label: C
options.text: Decreases labor productivity while increasing only nominal wages

options.label: D
options.text: Causes a movement along an unchanged PPC rather than changing capacity

options.label: E
options.text: Raises workers’ human capital and increases their productivity

explanation: Education can increase human capital, allowing workers to produce more output per unit of labor.

prompt: Government support for research that produces a more efficient production process will most directly

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease technology while shifting aggregate demand to the right

options.label: B
options.text: Increase technology and productivity, raising potential output

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the general price level without affecting real productive capacity

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce the amount of output obtainable from existing resources

options.label: E
options.text: Lower real GDP per capita by increasing the efficiency of production

explanation: A more efficient production process is a technological improvement.

prompt: If a policy raises labor-force participation while population and productivity remain unchanged, real GDP per capita will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease because the labor force is larger than before

options.label: B
options.text: Remain unchanged because productivity did not change

options.label: C
options.text: Increase only if the price level rises at the same time

options.label: D
options.text: Rises because more of the population contributes to production

options.label: E
options.text: Decrease because additional workers necessarily have zero output

explanation: With population fixed, a larger employed share increases total real output if productivity is positive.

prompt: Which statement best explains why supply-side fiscal policy can influence both the short run and the long run?

options.label: A
options.text: Affects current demand and incentives that shape future productive capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Supply-side fiscal policy changes only LRAS and can never affect aggregate demand

options.label: C
options.text: Supply-side fiscal policy changes only aggregate demand and leaves potential output fixed

options.label: D
options.text: All fiscal policy effects disappear immediately once the price level adjusts

options.label: E
options.text: Fiscal policy affects the money supply directly but cannot influence household or business incentives

explanation: Fiscal actions can change current spending, so they may shift aggregate demand in the short run. If they also alter incentives, productivity, labor participation, or capital formation, they can affect aggregate supply and potential output over time.

prompt: Which policy is more likely to raise long-run productive capacity than a one-time transfer payment of the same dollar amount?

options.label: A
options.text: Public investment that improves transportation infrastructure used by private firms

options.label: B
options.text: A one-time transfer that households spend entirely on existing consumer goods

options.label: C
options.text: A temporary rebate that raises consumption but does not alter productive incentives

options.label: D
options.text: A payment that changes nominal household income but leaves real resources unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: A transfer that raises aggregate demand for one period while potential output remains fixed

explanation: Infrastructure can raise productivity by lowering production and transportation costs, whereas a one-time transfer primarily supports current spending. The distinction is between increasing productive capacity and increasing demand for existing capacity.

prompt: A government builds a high-speed data network used by businesses. Which sequence best describes a plausible long-run effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Infrastructure improves → productivity falls → potential output falls → real GDP per capita rises

options.label: B
options.text: Infrastructure improves → price level rises → potential output is unchanged → real GDP per capita rises permanently

options.label: C
options.text: Infrastructure improves → labor-force participation must fall → potential output falls → growth accelerates

options.label: D
options.text: Infrastructure improves → productivity rises → potential output rises → real GDP per capita can increase

options.label: E
options.text: Infrastructure improves → money supply contracts → nominal interest rates rise → productive capacity necessarily falls

explanation: Useful infrastructure can increase the productivity of private labor and capital. That productivity gain expands potential output and can raise real GDP per capita over time.

prompt: Based on the graph above, which policy best explains the shift shown?

options.label: A
options.text: A temporary increase in aggregate demand that raises current output without changing capacity

options.label: B
options.text: A policy that increases unemployment while leaving resources and technology unchanged

options.label: C

prompt: A reduction in marginal income tax rates increases disposable income and also encourages greater labor-force participation. Which combination is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Aggregate demand decreases in the short run, and potential output necessarily decreases in the long run

options.label: B
options.text: Aggregate demand is unchanged because taxes affect only aggregate supply

options.label: C
options.text: Potential output increases only if the general price level also increases

options.label: D
options.text: Aggregate demand increases, but productive incentives cannot be affected by tax rates

options.label: E
options.text: Aggregate demand increases in the short run, and potential output can increase in the long run

explanation: Higher disposable income can raise consumption and aggregate demand in the short run. If lower marginal tax rates also encourage participation or work effort, the labor input and potential output can rise over time.

prompt: A policy raises labor productivity by 4 percent while population and labor-force participation are unchanged. Which outcome is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Real GDP per capita decreases because higher productivity reduces the need for labor

options.label: B
options.text: Real GDP per capita increases because each worker can produce more output

options.label: C
options.text: Real GDP per capita remains unchanged because the population did not change

options.label: D
options.text: Nominal GDP falls by 4 percent regardless of the price level

options.label: E
options.text: Potential output falls because the same output can be produced with fewer inputs

explanation: With participation and population fixed, higher productivity raises total real output. Because the same population shares a larger quantity of real output, real GDP per capita rises.

prompt: A public policy increases labor-force participation but leaves output per worker unchanged. Which statement best explains the growth effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Real GDP per capita must fall because more people are counted as workers

options.label: B
options.text: Higher employment can raise output per capita despite unchanged worker productivity

options.label: C
options.text: Potential output cannot change unless output per worker also rises

options.label: D
options.text: The policy affects only nominal GDP because labor participation is unrelated to real production

options.label: E
options.text: The policy shifts aggregate demand but cannot affect the economy’s productive capacity

explanation: Economic growth can arise from greater labor participation as well as higher productivity. If more of the population is employed at unchanged productivity, total output and output per person can rise.

prompt: A policy increases worker productivity but causes labor-force participation to decline. What can be concluded about the effect on real GDP per capita?

options.label: A
options.text: The effect is ambiguous without knowing the relative sizes of the productivity gain and participation decline

options.label: B
options.text: Real GDP per capita must increase because productivity is the only determinant that matters

options.label: C
options.text: Real GDP per capita must decrease because participation is the only determinant that matters

options.label: D
options.text: Real GDP per capita must remain unchanged because the two effects always offset exactly

options.label: E
options.text: Real GDP per capita can change only if the price level changes at the same time

explanation: Productivity and labor-force participation can both affect real output per person. When they move in opposite directions, the net effect depends on which change has the larger impact on production.

prompt: Based on the graph above, which policy could generate the shift from LRAS1 to LRAS2?

options.label: E

explanation: A higher labor-force participation rate can increase the labor available at full employment, raising potential output. That is represented by a rightward shift of LRAS.

prompt: An investment tax credit causes firms to purchase more equipment this year. Which pair of effects is most consistent with Topic 5.7?

prompt: A government technology program raises total factor productivity while aggregate demand is unchanged. Which long-run effect is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Potential output decreases because firms need fewer inputs per unit of output

options.label: B
options.text: Potential output remains fixed because only aggregate demand determines long-run output

options.label: C
options.text: The price level must increase while real GDP remains at its original potential level

options.label: D
options.text: Potential output increases because the economy can produce more with its resources

options.label: E
options.text: Labor-force participation must decline enough to offset the productivity gain

explanation: Higher total factor productivity increases the efficiency of the economy’s resources. This raises the sustainable level of real output and shifts LRAS to the right.

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a supply-side tax policy from a purely demand-oriented tax change?

options.label: A
options.text: A supply-side policy changes only government purchases and never tax rates

options.label: B
options.text: A supply-side policy affects only aggregate demand and cannot influence labor or investment decisions

options.label: C
options.text: A supply-side policy is implemented by the central bank rather than fiscal authorities

options.label: D
options.text: Changes productive incentives as well as current spending

options.label: E
options.text: A supply-side policy is defined by reducing the price level regardless of its incentive effects

explanation: Supply-side fiscal policy is distinguished by its intended effect on incentives that influence work, investment, and productive capacity. It may still have a demand-side effect through disposable income or investment spending.
